prompt: Which market structure is characterised by many firms selling an identical product with no significant barriers to entry?

options.label: A
options.text: Monopoly

options.label: B
options.text: Monopolistic competition

options.label: C
options.text: Oligopoly

options.label: D
options.text: Perfect competition

explanation: Perfect competition has many buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product and free entry. No individual firm has market power.

prompt: Which market structure has a single supplier protected by high barriers to entry?

options.label: A
options.text: Perfect competition

options.label: B
options.text: Monopolistic competition

options.label: C
options.text: Contestable competition

options.label: D
options.text: Monopoly

explanation: A pure monopoly consists of one firm in the industry, with barriers that prevent or strongly discourage entry by rivals.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.1 perfect competition and imperfect competition: monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, natural monopoly | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which market structure is most closely associated with many firms selling differentiated products and relatively low barriers to entry?

options.label: A
options.text: Monopolistic competition

options.label: B
options.text: Perfect competition

options.label: C
options.text: Monopoly

options.label: D
options.text: Natural monopoly

explanation: Monopolistic competition combines many sellers and relatively free entry with product differentiation, giving each firm some market power.

prompt: Which feature best distinguishes oligopoly from monopolistic competition?

options.label: A
options.text: A few dominant firms with strategic interdependence.

options.label: B
options.text: Many small firms sell differentiated products and respond only to consumer demand, not rivals’ strategic decisions.

options.label: C
options.text: Unrestricted entry with no sunk costs.

options.label: D
options.text: Price-taking firms facing horizontal demand curves.

explanation: Oligopoly is characterised by market concentration in the hands of a few firms. Monopolistic competition normally contains many competing sellers.

prompt: When is an industry most likely to be a natural monopoly?

options.label: A
options.text: Strong brand loyalty makes one firm a natural monopoly even when several producers could supply demand more cheaply.

options.label: B
options.text: Many small suppliers have identical average production costs.

options.label: C
options.text: One supplier serves total demand at lowest average cost.

options.label: D
options.text: Entry and exit impose no costs on firms.

explanation: A natural monopoly arises when economies of scale are so extensive that a single supplier can serve the market at lower average cost than multiple suppliers.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.1 perfect competition and imperfect competition: monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, natural monopoly | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: A firm in perfect competition is described as a price taker because

options.label: A
options.text: A law prevents the firm from changing prices.

options.label: B
options.text: Its marginal cost equals zero at every output.

options.label: C
options.text: Its product faces no close competing suppliers.

options.label: D
options.text: Its small market share prevents it influencing price.

explanation: With many small firms selling an identical product, one firm cannot affect the market price and must accept the price determined by market demand and supply.

prompt: Which feature is most consistent with monopoly rather than perfect competition?

options.label: A
options.text: Perfect information

options.label: B
options.text: Many competing firms with unrestricted entry into the industry

options.label: C
options.text: A homogeneous product

options.label: D
options.text: High barriers to entry

explanation: High barriers protect a monopolist from entry. Perfect competition instead requires freedom of entry and exit.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.2 structure of the listed markets: number of buyers and sellers, product differentiation, degree of freedom of entry and availability of information | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which is a legal barrier to entry?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumer loyalty built through a firm’s advertising campaign and the reputation of its established product brand.

options.label: B
options.text: Large production scale reducing incumbents’ average costs.

options.label: C

prompt: Which is most clearly a market barrier to entry?

options.label: A
options.text: A government licence restricting the number of providers

options.label: B
options.text: Strong consumer loyalty to established brands

options.label: C
options.text: A very large minimum efficient scale

options.label: D
options.text: Exclusive ownership of a mineral deposit

explanation: Brand loyalty and established reputation make it difficult for entrants to win customers even when entry is legally possible.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.3 barriers to entry and exit: market barriers | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which is most clearly a cost barrier to entry?

options.label: A
options.text: Patent protection preventing imitation of the incumbent’s process.

options.label: B
options.text: Scale economies giving the incumbent lower unit costs.

options.label: C
options.text: Exclusive control of the only suitable harbour site.

options.label: D
options.text: Brand loyalty making consumers reluctant to try new suppliers.

explanation: Economies of scale can make a new small entrant a high-cost producer relative to an established large firm.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.3 barriers to entry and exit: cost barriers | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which is most clearly a physical barrier to entry?

options.label: A
options.text: Advertising creates strong consumer loyalty to existing brands.

options.label: B
options.text: A patent prevents imitation of existing production technology.

options.label: C
options.text: An incumbent controls the only suitable terminal site.

options.label: D
options.text: Large fixed expenditure is required before production begins.

reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.3 barriers to entry and exit: physical barriers | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A perfectly competitive firm faces a horizontal demand curve at the market price. Which relationship follows?

options.label: A
options.text: AR > MR > price

options.label: B
options.text: AR = MR = price

options.label: C
options.text: MR > AR = price

options.label: D
options.text: AR = price > MR

explanation: The firm can sell each additional unit at the unchanged market price. Therefore average revenue, marginal revenue and price are equal.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.4 performance of firms: revenues and revenue curves | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Why is the demand curve facing a monopolist downward sloping?

options.label: A
options.text: The firm must accept the prevailing market price.

options.label: B
options.text: Extra sales generally require a lower selling price.

options.label: C
options.text: Marginal production costs fall whenever output is increased.

options.label: D
options.text: Unrestricted entry makes every product perfectly substitutable.

explanation: The monopolist is the industry supplier, so its demand curve is the market demand curve. More output normally requires a lower price.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.4 performance of firms: revenues and revenue curves | AO2 Analysis

prompt: For a firm facing a normal downward-sloping demand curve, marginal revenue is normally

options.label: A
options.text: Below average revenue.

options.label: B
options.text: Above average revenue at every output.

options.label: C
options.text: Equal to average revenue at every output.

options.label: D
options.text: Unrelated to total revenue.

explanation: When price must be lowered to sell an additional unit, the extra revenue from that unit is less than the new price, so MR lies below AR.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.4 performance of firms: revenues and revenue curves | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which profit outcome is possible for a perfectly competitive firm in the short run?

options.label: A
options.text: Only normal profit is possible.

options.label: B
options.text: Only supernormal profit is possible.

options.label: C
options.text: Normal, supernormal or subnormal profit.

options.label: D
options.text: Only subnormal profit is possible.

explanation: In the short run the market price can lie above, equal to or below average total cost, so all three profit outcomes are possible.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.4 performance of firms: profits in the short run and the long run | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Why is supernormal profit competed away in long-run perfect competition?

options.label: A
options.text: Collusion reduces output and raises market prices.

options.label: B
options.text: Government intervention sets product prices to zero.

options.label: C
options.text: Entry expands supply and lowers market prices.

options.label: D
options.text: Differentiation reduces substitutability between firms’ products.

explanation: Free entry means supernormal profit attracts entrants. The resulting increase in market supply pushes price down until firms earn normal profit.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.4 performance of firms: profits in the short run and the long run | 7.6.4 performance of firms: output in the short run and the long run | AO2 Analysis

prompt: What is the short-run shutdown rule for a perfectly competitive firm?

options.label: A
options.text: Shut down when P is below ATC.

options.label: B
options.text: Shut down when MC is rising.

options.label: C
options.text: Shut down when P is above AVC.

options.label: D
options.text: Shut down when P is below AVC.

explanation: In the short run, fixed costs must be paid whether the firm produces or not. Production continues if revenue covers variable cost; if price is below AVC, producing increases the loss.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.4 performance of firms: shutdown price in the short run and the long run | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: In the long run, a firm will leave an industry if

options.label: A
options.text: AVC exceeds price for one day only.

options.label: B
options.text: MC rises at the chosen output level.

options.label: C
options.text: TR falls short of total economic cost.

options.label: D
options.text: Fixed costs remain positive at the chosen output.

explanation: All costs are avoidable in the long run. A firm must cover total economic cost, including normal profit, to remain in the industry.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.4 performance of firms: shutdown price in the short run and the long run | AO2 Analysis

prompt: The short-run supply curve of a perfectly competitive firm is the portion of its

options.label: A
options.text: ATC at and above minimum AVC.

options.label: B
options.text: MR at and above minimum ATC.

options.label: C
options.text: MC at and above minimum AVC.

options.label: D
options.text: AR at and above minimum MC.

explanation: At each viable market price, the firm supplies the output where price equals marginal cost, provided price is high enough to cover AVC. Hence MC above minimum AVC is the short-run supply curve.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.4 performance of firms: derivation of a firm’s supply curve in a perfectly competitive market | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: A perfectly competitive firm has no externalities and is allocatively efficient when

options.label: A
options.text: Where P equals AR.

options.label: B
options.text: Where P equals MC.

options.label: C
options.text: Where AC is falling.

options.label: D
options.text: Where MR equals zero.

explanation: Allocative efficiency requires the marginal value consumers place on output, represented by price, to equal marginal cost.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.4 performance of firms: efficiency and X-inefficiency in the short run and the long run | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: A firm is productively efficient when it produces

options.label: A
options.text: At the highest attainable selling price.

options.label: B
options.text: At the minimum attainable average cost.

options.label: C
options.text: At the zero-marginal-revenue output.

options.label: D
options.text: At the minimum possible market output.

explanation: Productive efficiency means output is produced at the lowest attainable average cost.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.4 performance of firms: efficiency and X-inefficiency in the short run and the long run | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: What is X-inefficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Avoidable production costs arising from weak competitive pressure.

options.label: B
options.text: Lower average costs arising from large production scale.

options.label: C
options.text: Below-marginal-cost prices arising from intense competition.

options.label: D
options.text: Product shortages arising from binding maximum prices.

explanation: X-inefficiency is organisational slack or poor cost control that leaves actual costs above the minimum attainable level.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.4 performance of firms: efficiency and X-inefficiency in the short run and the long run | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which feature is essential for a highly contestable market?

options.label: A
options.text: Many established firms compete while every potential entrant must incur large costs that cannot be recovered on exit.

options.label: B
options.text: Easy entry and exit with low sunk costs.

options.label: C
options.text: Identical products alongside substantial legal barriers.

options.label: D
options.text: Government ownership alongside substantial physical barriers.

explanation: Contestability depends on the ease with which potential rivals can enter and leave. Even a concentrated market can be contestable if entry and exit are sufficiently easy.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.4 performance of firms: contestable markets, features and implications | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Why can the threat of entry discipline a monopolist in a contestable market?

options.label: A
options.text: Potential entry legally turns the incumbent into a price taker.

options.label: B
options.text: High profits may attract entrants that undercut the incumbent.

options.label: C
options.text: Potential entry eliminates all production economies enjoyed by the incumbent.

options.label: D
options.text: High profits necessarily make the incumbent’s demand perfectly inelastic.

explanation: Potential competition can constrain an incumbent even before entry occurs, because excessive price or profit creates an opportunity for hit-and-run entry.

prompt: Which is an example of non-price competition?

prompt: Why is non-price competition especially common in monopolistic competition?

prompt: Collusion between oligopolists aims to

options.label: A
options.text: Eliminate barriers preventing the entry of potential rivals.

options.label: B

prompt: A perfectly competitive firm has price $14, AVC $11 and ATC $17 at its profit-maximising output. What should it do in the short run?

options.label: A
options.text: Shut down because price is below ATC.

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Exit immediately because fixed costs are avoidable.

options.label: D
options.text: Raise price because the firm controls market price.

prompt: A perfectly competitive firm has price $9 and minimum AVC $10. What is the short-run decision?

prompt: A perfectly competitive firm has price $24 and minimum ATC $24 in the long run. What profit does it earn?

options.label: C

options.label: D

prompt: A concentration ratio falls after several foreign firms begin supplying the domestic market. What does this most directly indicate?

options.label: A
options.text: Entry barriers necessarily become higher.

options.label: B
options.text: Every domestic firm now earns exactly normal profit because foreign suppliers’ entry eliminates all possible profit differences.

options.label: C
options.text: Price competition necessarily disappears.

options.label: D
options.text: The largest domestic firms lose combined market share.

explanation: The ratio is a market-share measure. A fall means the specified leading firms command a smaller combined share, though it does not by itself reveal profit or price behaviour.

prompt:
Consider this pay-off matrix, where entries are profits for A/B. What is the Nash outcome if each firm chooses its best response?
| Firm A’s choice | B: High | B: Low |
| A: High | 45 / 45 | 20 / 60 |
| A: Low | 60 / 20 | 30 / 30 |

options.label: A
options.text: Both choose High.

options.label: B
options.text: Both choose Low.

options.label: C
options.text: A chooses High and B chooses Low.

options.label: D
options.text: A chooses Low and B chooses High.

explanation: For A, Low gives 60 rather than 45 if B chooses High, and 30 rather than 20 if B chooses Low. By symmetry B also prefers Low in either case. Thus Low/Low is the mutual best-response outcome.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.4 performance of firms: collusion and the Prisoner’s Dilemma in oligopolistic markets, including a two-player pay-off matrix | AO2 Analysis

prompt:
Using the pay-off matrix below, why is the Low/Low outcome a Prisoner’s Dilemma?
| Firm A’s choice | B: High | B: Low |
| A: High | 45 / 45 | 20 / 60 |
| A: Low | 60 / 20 | 30 / 30 |

options.label: A
options.text: Low/Low maximises the firms’ combined profits.

options.label: B
options.text: Neither firm can change its chosen strategy, even when switching from High to Low would raise its own profit.

options.label: C
options.text: High/High is each firm’s dominant strategy.

options.label: D
options.text: Individual incentives undermine the jointly preferable High/High outcome.

explanation: High/High gives combined profit 90 compared with 60 at Low/Low, but each firm can raise its own profit from 45 to 60 by deviating when the other stays High. Cooperation is therefore difficult to sustain.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.4 performance of firms: collusion and the Prisoner’s Dilemma in oligopolistic markets, including a two-player pay-off matrix | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A repeated-game setting makes future retaliation possible if one oligopolist breaks an agreement. How can this affect the Prisoner’s Dilemma?

options.label: A
options.text: Future punishment necessarily establishes perfect competition.

options.label: B
options.text: Expected punishment may make cooperation more sustainable.

options.label: C
options.text: Future punishment removes strategic interdependence between firms.

options.label: D
options.text: Expected punishment makes every possible strategy dominant.

explanation: When firms interact repeatedly, the value of future cooperation and the threat of retaliation can reduce the incentive to defect from a collusive arrangement.

prompt: Two oligopolists are considering an advertising campaign rather than a price cut. Which feature of oligopoly makes the decision strategic?

options.label: A
options.text: Each firm lacks any influence over market outcomes.

options.label: B
options.text: Each potential entrant faces no barriers to entry.

options.label: C
options.text: Each firm’s payoff depends on its rival’s choices.

options.label: D
options.text: Each firm supplies a product identical to its rivals’.

explanation: Oligopolistic interdependence means the profitability of one firm’s action depends on the response chosen by rivals.

prompt: An oligopolist cuts price and rivals immediately match the cut. What is the most likely direct effect on the original firm’s market share and industry profit, other things equal?

options.label: A
options.text: Its share doubles; total industry profit rises.

options.label: B
options.text: Its share becomes zero; industry profit stays unchanged.

options.label: C
options.text: Every firm becomes a price taker permanently.

options.label: D
options.text: Little share gain; potentially lower industry profits.

explanation: If rivals match the price cut, the initiating firm may gain little lasting share, while lower prices reduce margins across the industry.
reference: 7.6 Different market structures | 7.6.4 performance of firms: price competition and non-price competition | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A monopolistically competitive firm successfully differentiates its product so consumers see fewer close substitutes. What is the most likely short-run effect?

options.label: A
options.text: Less elastic demand may increase market power.

options.label: B
options.text: Differentiation necessarily makes demand perfectly price elastic.

options.label: C
options.text: All existing entry barriers become legal restrictions.

options.label: D
options.text: Differentiation necessarily establishes a perfectly competitive market.

explanation: Stronger differentiation and brand loyalty make consumers less responsive to price and give the firm greater discretion over price.

prompt: Why does long-run normal profit in monopolistic competition not imply productive efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal profit requires price to equal marginal cost.

options.label: B
options.text: Normal profit requires demand to be perfectly elastic.

options.label: C
options.text: Normal profit eliminates differences between firms’ products.

options.label: D
options.text: Normal profit is possible below minimum AC output.

explanation: Entry can reduce profit to normal while a differentiated firm still operates with excess capacity, so normal profit and productive efficiency are distinct concepts.

prompt: A natural monopoly is required to charge a price equal to marginal cost, but at that output price lies below average cost. What follows?

options.label: A
options.text: Economic profit necessarily becomes positive.

options.label: B
options.text: A loss requires subsidy or alternative pricing.

options.label: C
options.text: Average cost immediately falls below marginal cost.

options.label: D
options.text: The market necessarily becomes perfectly competitive.

explanation: With substantial fixed infrastructure costs, marginal-cost pricing can set revenue below total cost. The natural monopoly may then require subsidy or an alternative pricing rule.

prompt: Compare a profit-maximising, single-price monopolist with a competitive market facing the same downward-sloping demand and upward-sloping marginal cost. Assume interior solutions and no externalities. What is the monopoly outcome relative to competition?

options.label: A
options.text: A lower price and a higher output.

options.label: B
options.text: The same price and a lower output.

options.label: C
options.text: A higher price and a lower output.

options.label: D
options.text: A higher price and the same output.

explanation: The monopolist chooses MR = MC, then charges the price on demand. Competition produces where P = MC. With the stated common demand and cost conditions, monopoly output is lower and its price is higher. This comparison does not establish which has higher average cost.

prompt: A firm in a highly contestable market considers raising price to earn supernormal profit. Why might it choose not to?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand must be perfectly price elastic.

options.label: B
options.text: Positive economic profit is legally prohibited.

options.label: C
options.text: Profits may attract hit-and-run entrants.

options.label: D
options.text: Fixed costs automatically become variable costs.

explanation: Potential entrants are drawn by profitable opportunities. The threat of entry can therefore limit the incumbent’s price even without current rivals.

prompt: A market is opened to entry, but every entrant must build a dedicated network that cannot be resold. Why may deregulation have little effect on contestability?

options.label: A
options.text: Unrecoverable network expenditure remains an entry barrier.

options.label: B
options.text: A large consumer population prevents successful market entry.

options.label: C
options.text: Product differentiation alone makes the market uncontestable.

options.label: D
options.text: Readily available information prevents entrants assessing the market.

explanation: Removing a legal restriction is not enough if cost barriers remain. Large sunk costs can still deter entry and make exit expensive.
